briefing: The Bank of Canada raised its key rate to 2.50%, its first hike since 2023, and Premier Doug Ford called it a massive mistake, while the U.S. Federal Reserve held at 3.75% to 4% with two officials voting for a hike. Oil stays near US$115 on reports Washington told Gulf allies to prepare for strikes on Iran after the midterms. Ontario matched Ottawa's capital-investment tax break a day before Thursday's fall economic statement, and Canadian ministers doubt Trump will bend on auto tariffs.

stories.backstory: Oil prices jumped after the U.S.-Iran war closed much of the Strait of Hormuz earlier this year, and fuel costs have fed through to inflation since. The Bank of Canada cut its rate to 2.25% in October 2025 and then held for seven meetings while weighing whether the energy spike would fade. September inflation reached 3.1%, driven by a 27.8% jump in gasoline prices, even as Canada lost 68,000 jobs and unemployment rose to 6.5%. By last week most economists and traders expected a hike.
stories.headline: Bank of Canada hikes to 2.50%, its first increase since 2023
stories.impact: Big banks' prime rates usually rise by the same quarter point within a day or two, so variable-rate mortgages, HELOCs and lines of credit will cost more; fixed-rate holders are unaffected until renewal. Anyone renewing a GTA mortgage soon should budget for possibly another hike, while savings and GIC rates may tick up.
stories.now: At 9:45 a.m. the Bank of Canada lifted its policy rate from 2.25% to 2.50%, its first hike since July 2023, to keep high oil prices from spreading into other prices, and said a further increase could be needed. Its new forecast puts 2027 inflation at 3.1%, up from 2.0% in July, with growth of 1.0% this year and 2.0% next. The bank also warned of a subdued housing market as affordability, slower population growth and higher borrowing costs weigh on sales and construction; Royal LePage CEO Phil Soper said the key question is whether this is a one-off or the start of a tightening cycle. Ford said higher rates won't fix oil supply or tariffs and will only raise costs for families, while Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy noted the bank is independent. In the afternoon the U.S. Federal Reserve held its own rate steady.

stories.backstory: The U.S. and Israel began striking Iran on February 28, 2026, in the middle of nuclear talks. The first wave killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. Iran answered with missiles and drones on Israel, Gulf states and U.S. bases, and closed the Strait of Hormuz, the channel that roughly a fifth of the world's oil normally passes through. A peace memorandum signed in June briefly reopened shipping, but it fell apart in July when Iran started attacking commercial ships again to press its claim over the strait.
stories.headline: Oil near US$115 after Houthis claim hit on Saudi Arabia's biggest refinery
stories.impact: This is the main reason gas and diesel in Ontario stay expensive: GTA regular has been forecast around $1.80 a litre and diesel near $2.65. A strike after November 3 could lift pump prices again and complicate the Bank of Canada's inflation fight.
stories.now: Yemen's Houthis claimed a ballistic-missile strike on Ras Tanura, Saudi Arabia's largest refinery at about 550,000 barrels a day; Bloomberg reported a fire near the export terminal that was later contained, and Saudi authorities have not confirmed damage, though the coalition says it intercepted three missiles and four drones. Qatar's draft deal, delivered Sunday, sets out a seven-day sequence of daily confidence-building steps with outside guarantors, but a senior Iranian official told Reuters it contained unacceptable ideas, and Tehran wants the U.S. port blockade and oil sanctions lifted first, while Washington wants the nuclear program on the table from the start. U.S. Naval Forces Central Command told ships with no need to transit the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman to stay well clear. Brent rose about 1% to roughly US$115 a barrel and U.S. crude (WTI) 1.8% to about US$101.70 on Wednesday, after a report that Washington told Gulf states to prepare for post-midterm strikes on Iran.

stories.backstory: The U.S. Supreme Court struck down Trump's broad emergency tariffs in February, but sector tariffs on steel, aluminum, autos, copper and lumber stayed. At the first CUSMA review on July 1, the U.S. refused to extend the deal for a full new term, so it now needs annual reviews. Ottawa walked out of talks on August 21, calling Washington's last-minute demands unfair. The U.S. imposed 50% tariffs on August 22, and Canada matched with counter-tariffs on September 8, plus a $25B support package for affected workers and businesses.
stories.headline: Ministers doubt Trump will bend on autos as envoy's warning stings
stories.impact: Ontario manufacturers of flooring, carpets, paints and personal-care products face a 50% U.S. tariff from Friday, which could mean layoffs or reduced shifts. A real deal would matter most for GTA auto, steel and aluminum jobs, which are not yet covered by any relief.
stories.now: Ministers briefed on the faster pace of talks told CTV News they are skeptical Trump will make the concessions needed, with one saying trust is gone after talks collapsed in August; autos, which Carney calls a red line, are the hardest issue, while sources expect U.S. movement on culture and Canada's freedom to trade with others. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick restarted talks last week, focused on the Section 232 tariffs on steel, aluminum and autos, and chief negotiator Janice Charette has warned businesses some tariffs will stay even with a deal. Hoekstra reportedly told an off-the-record Ottawa lunch on Tuesday that Canada could be blamed if Republicans lose in Michigan and Maine; the U.S. embassy says the remarks were taken out of context. New 50% U.S. tariffs on Canadian flooring, carpets, shampoos, soaps and cocoa products start Friday, October 30, and Canada's counter-tariffs remain.

stories.backstory: The spring 2026 budget pushed Ontario's target for balancing the books back to 2028-29. U.S. tariffs of up to 50% on Canadian goods have hit the province's steel, auto and lumber industries hardest. Fall economic statements update the budget's numbers and often add targeted tax or spending changes. This week Ottawa and Ontario announced an $8.7-billion plan for steel, autos and Ring of Fire roads.
stories.headline: Ontario matches Ottawa's investment tax break a day before fiscal update
stories.impact: The tax break targets manufacturers and other firms investing in equipment, which could help protect GTA factory jobs hit by tariffs. Students at private career colleges still face an OSAP freeze until 2027, and any restraint in Thursday's update could reach health, education and transit.
stories.now: Ontario will match Ottawa's measure letting businesses immediately deduct the full cost of eligible machinery, equipment and technology, which Prime Minister Mark Carney expanded last month to cover about two-thirds of assets. Bethlenfalvy says the change provides about $8 billion in relief and lowers Ontario's marginal effective tax rate on new investment to 3.6%. Meanwhile Career Colleges Ontario says Better Jobs Ontario retraining funding for unemployed people has been paused without notice, on top of the OSAP freeze for private career colleges; the ministry says other funding is under review. The fall economic statement is tabled Thursday, with the deficit last forecast near $13.8 billion.

stories.backstory: Republicans have controlled both the House and Senate since January 2025, which has let Trump pass his agenda with few checks. Midterms usually go against the president's party, and Trump's approval is lower than at the same point in his first term. All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are on the ballot. A Democratic House could launch investigations and block spending and trade legislation.
stories.headline: New polls show tight Senate races in Ohio, Texas and South Carolina
stories.impact: A change in Congress could shift the odds of tariff relief for Ontario's auto, steel and lumber industries. Ottawa's trade strategy is partly being timed around the outcome.
stories.now: A Reuters/Ipsos poll taken October 22–26 has Democrats ahead by nine points, 50% to 41% with leaners, on which party voters back for Congress. A Suffolk University poll in Ohio has former Senator Sherrod Brown at 47% to Senator Jon Husted's 44%, a New York Times/Siena poll shows South Carolina's Senate race tied at 48% each, and Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton is roughly even with Democrat James Talarico. Trump holds a rally Wednesday evening in Chillicothe, Ohio, his third Ohio stop this month, while former President Barack Obama campaigns in Atlanta with Senator Jon Ossoff and Vice President JD Vance speaks in North Carolina. Republicans hold the Senate 53-47, and the Cook Political Report rates the House as leaning Democratic and the Senate a toss-up.

stories.backstory: Tech giants have poured hundreds of billions of dollars into data centres and chips for AI, and those stocks have driven much of the market's gains. Investors have swung between excitement and doubt about whether the spending will pay off. This year's oil shock from the Iran war has also kept inflation and interest-rate worries alive.
stories.headline: Fed holds at 3.75%–4% as two officials vote for a hike
stories.impact: Fixed mortgage rates in Canada follow bond yields, which take cues from the Fed, so a hawkish Fed adds pressure on top of the Bank of Canada's hike. Ontario RRSPs, TFSAs and pensions that hold U.S. tech will feel tonight's earnings.
stories.now: The Fed kept its benchmark range at 3.75% to 4%, after raising it in September for the first time in three years. Cook, in her first policy dissent, and Hammack both wanted a hike, and the statement upgraded the economy to 'strong' while saying more information will help decide the next move, which Reuters read as a hint of guidance Chair Kevin Warsh has said he prefers to avoid. U.S. inflation is running near 3.7%, about a point above target, with oil above US$100 a barrel, and traders still see a real chance of a December hike. Microsoft and Alphabet report earnings after the close, with investors watching whether heavy AI spending is paying off.

stories.backstory: This is Israel's first national election since the Hamas attack of October 7, 2023, and the long Gaza war that followed. Netanyahu, the country's longest-serving prime minister, leads a coalition of Likud with ultra-Orthodox and far-right parties and is still on trial for corruption, which he denies. The opposition has campaigned on accountability for the security failures before October 7, while the war with Iran and the military-service exemption for ultra-Orthodox men are also major issues. In Israel the biggest party does not automatically govern; whoever can assemble 61 seats forms the government.
stories.headline: Netanyahu's bloc holds at 54 seats as Eisenkot's bloc rises to 49
stories.impact: For Ontario residents the main link is energy: Netanyahu has pushed for renewed strikes on Iran, and the next government's stance could move crude and GTA pump prices. The vote also matters to many Jewish, Arab and Muslim families in the GTA with ties to the region.
stories.now: The latest partial results reported by the Times of Israel and Ynet give the pro-Netanyahu bloc 54 seats, Gadi Eisenkot's opposition bloc 49 and the Arab-led parties 17, after earlier tallies had the opposition at 47 and Arab parties at 19. Likud remains the largest party at roughly 27 seats, ahead of Eisenkot's Yashar at about 21. Netanyahu says he wants a right-wing government and will not rely on Arab parties, while Democrats leader Yair Golan has urged the opposition to work with them. Some 600,000 to 650,000 double-envelope ballots, including soldiers' and diplomats' votes, still need to be verified, possibly into Friday, and final results are due Nov. 4, after which President Isaac Herzog consults the parties.

stories.backstory: Cleveland-Cliffs, an Ohio steelmaker, bought Hamilton-based Stelco in 2024, and Ottawa approved the deal on condition that union jobs and most non-union roles be kept. U.S. 50% tariffs on Canadian steel since August have hit exports hard. In early October Stelco announced a partial shutdown of finishing lines at Hamilton Works, cutting up to 500 jobs, and Joly gave the company five days to respond. The dispute has become a test of whether Ottawa can enforce foreign-takeover promises.
stories.headline: Joly won't meet Stelco owner's CEO without a plan to restore jobs
stories.impact: Hundreds of Hamilton families face lost paycheques, with knock-on effects for suppliers and the local economy. The outcome may shape whether the new federal-Ontario steel fund keeps similar plants running.
stories.now: Joly wants Cleveland-Cliffs, which bought Hamilton-based Stelco in 2024, to answer six alleged breaches of its binding commitments, including keeping union jobs at the same level for five years, and has said Ottawa could go to court, seek penalties or force a sale. Her earlier letter gave the company 15 days to comply; up to 500 jobs at the Hamilton and Lake Erie operations are affected, and about 200 workers have been laid off. Cleveland-Cliffs says it meets all 34 of its undertakings and will update its compliance report after the reporting period ends October 31; Goncalves blames imports of galvanized steel. Premier Doug Ford and the steelworkers' union back Ottawa's push.

stories.backstory: Chow first won a 2023 by-election with 37% after John Tory resigned, and this was her first run as an incumbent. Bradford, a Beaches-East York councillor, ran on a first-year property-tax freeze and scrapping Toronto's land transfer tax on homes under $1.1 million, while Chow promised cheaper groceries, school lunches and more affordable housing. Mississauga's race pitted Parrish, elected in a 2024 by-election, against Crombie, who returned after leading the Ontario Liberals. All Ontario municipalities voted on the same day for four-year terms.
stories.headline: Chow re-elected; GTA voters oust mayors in Mississauga, Hamilton, Oakville and Milton
stories.impact: Toronto homeowners should expect Chow's budget approach to continue rather than Bradford's proposed tax freeze, and Mississauga residents can watch for Tedjo's promised two-year freeze on the residential tax levy. Ward councillor and school trustee results are posted on each city's website.
stories.now: Chow finished with about 54% to Brad Bradford's 41%, a margin of more than 127,000 votes, and carried 19 of Toronto's 25 wards after polls had suggested a close race; ballots counted by 10 p.m. were roughly double the 563,124 cast in 2022. Alvin Tedjo unseated Carolyn Parrish in Mississauga, and in Hamilton Keanin Loomis won with about 41% while Andrea Horwath fell to third at 14%. In Halton, Jeff Knoll took Oakville with 36% over incumbent Rob Burton, and George Minakakis beat Milton's long-time mayor Gord Krantz 45% to about 25%; Christina Early won Caledon with 59%. Patrick Brown (Brampton), Steven Del Duca (Vaughan), Frank Scarpitti (Markham) and David West (Richmond Hill) were re-elected, while Oshawa, Clarington and Ajax chose new mayors.

stories.backstory: Russia's full-scale invasion is in its fifth year. Trump's envoys have made several trips to Moscow, while Zelenskyy has pushed for a leaders' meeting that Russia rejects. Russia has been pounding Ukraine's power grid ahead of winter, and Kyiv has struck Russian refineries in return. Ukraine has also complained about U.S. limits on intelligence sharing and a Starlink slowdown.
stories.headline: Russia and Ukraine trade overnight drone strikes as UN panel condemns grid attacks
stories.impact: Canada is a major Ukraine backer and is being asked for more money at the October 29–30 Canada-EU summit, which affects federal spending. Any real progress toward peace could ease diesel and gas prices over time.
stories.now: Overnight into Wednesday, Russia launched one ballistic missile and 88 attack drones; Ukraine's Air Force said 71 drones were downed, while hits were recorded at eight locations, and a strike in Kharkiv injured five people, including a four-year-old. Local authorities say Russian attacks killed 2 people and injured 17 across Ukraine over the past day. Ukrainian drones struck Russia's Tula region, where the governor reported damage in Novomoskovsk. A U.S.-brokered ceasefire around occupied Oleshky, in effect until Nov. 1 to allow aid and evacuations, passed its first 30 hours without an incident, according to Ukraine's human rights ombudsman. On Tuesday, a UN Commission of Inquiry said Russia's attacks on Ukraine's power grid amount to a crime against humanity.

stories.backstory: Since U.S. tariffs hit Canadian steel, aluminum, autos and lumber, Carney has pushed to sell more to other markets. Canada and the EU already trade under the CETA free-trade deal, and in February 2026 Canada became the first non-European country to join the EU's SAFE defence-procurement program. Ottawa has also been courting Gulf investors and, separately, is racing to finish a trade deal with India before Modi's December visit.

stories.impact: Projects such as Ontario's Ring of Fire mining region depend on First Nations agreements, which affects future jobs and investment in the province. Few immediate effects for GTA households.
stories.now: Two European sources told CTV News the 'associate member' label, floated by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, is not in the draft statement for this week's summit with Prime Minister Mark Carney; Politico first reported it. Germany has raised concerns about the term, and the draft has changed many times and could change again. The summit is instead expected to launch further talks on a deeper partnership, with details on any closer status expected next year. Earlier this week Canada signed a partnership with the United Arab Emirates in Ottawa.

stories.backstory: MAID has been legal in Canada since 2016, and the rules were widened in 2021 to include people whose death is not reasonably foreseeable. Extending it to mental illness alone was delayed several times amid concerns about assessing such cases. A special joint committee of MPs and senators recommended in June that those cases be excluded indefinitely, and Quebec already allows advance requests under its own law.
stories.headline: Ottawa tables bill to bar MAID for mental illness alone, allow advance requests
stories.impact: For Ontario families, any advance-request option would depend on whether Queen's Park chooses to allow it under provincial health rules. People whose sole condition is a mental illness would remain ineligible if the bill passes.
stories.now: Justice Minister Sean Fraser introduced Bill C-41 on Tuesday. It removes the expansion that would otherwise take effect March 17, when people whose sole condition is mental illness would become eligible, so it must pass the House and Senate before then. It also changes the Criminal Code to permit advance requests for people with degenerative illnesses such as dementia or ALS, which two independent doctors or nurse practitioners must approve. MAID could not go ahead if the person later resists through words, sounds or gestures, and each province would decide whether to offer advance requests.

stories.backstory: Comey led the FBI until Trump fired him in 2017 and has been a frequent Trump critic. He was indicted in September 2025 on charges of lying to Congress, but a judge dismissed that case in November 2025, ruling the prosecutor who brought it was unlawfully appointed; the government appealed. In April 2026 he was charged again in North Carolina over a social media photo of seashells spelling '86 47', which Trump called a threat. Critics say the cases show the Justice Department being used against the president's opponents, while the administration says no one is above the law.
stories.headline: Justice Department charges James Comey a third time
stories.impact: There is little direct effect on daily life in Ontario. It matters for Canadians watching U.S. institutions, since the independence of American courts and prosecutors shapes how predictable Washington is as a trade and security partner.
stories.now: A charging document unsealed Monday in federal court in Washington, D.C., accuses Comey of directing someone to share national defence information with a reporter in October 2016, plus a conspiracy count; reports link it to a 2016 New York Times article. The document does not name the reporter or the alleged co-conspirator, and Judge Trevor McFadden ordered it unsealed. Comey called the case an abuse of the Justice Department and says he is innocent; his lawyer, Patrick Fitzgerald, argues the 10-year time limit expired October 5 and notes the government previously chose not to charge anyone over the same story. The same day, a federal judge ruled that the firing of Comey's daughter Maurene as a Manhattan federal prosecutor was unlawful; the department plans to appeal.

stories.backstory: 55 Division covers much of Toronto's east end, including Riverdale, Leslieville and the Beaches. Police have run several targeted gun-and-drug projects in recent years as gun violence remains a top concern for residents. Fentanyl continues to drive overdose deaths across the city, and illegal handguns are mostly smuggled in from the U.S. Such projects usually run for months before arrests are announced together.
stories.headline: Toronto police arrest 44 in east-end guns and drugs probe
stories.impact: East-end Toronto residents may see fewer illegal guns and drug sales in the area. Police ask anyone with information to call 416-808-5500.
stories.now: Toronto police say Project Matrix, launched March 1 by 55 Division's major crime unit, targeted illegal guns, drug trafficking and related crime in the city's east end. Officers arrested 44 people and laid 187 charges. Seizures included eight illegal firearms, 792 rounds of ammunition, and cocaine, methamphetamine, fentanyl, MDMA and other drugs. The most common charges were probation breaches, unsafe firearm storage and possession for trafficking, and police say the investigation continues.
